32.1812 119.808 36.6905 124.717 36.6905Z"></path></svg></span><span>Data</span></a></li></ul></div></nav></aside><article class="px-6 md:px-12 overflow-x-visible"><div class="max-w-[var(--content-width)] mx-auto overflow-visible"><div class="prose"><p>Jev (<span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="https://docs.typesafe.ai/models" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="">TypeSafe&#x27;s system-one model</a></span>) is a quantum leap forward for data processing pipelines, if harnessed correctly. We used Jev to accelerate an entity resolution pipeline to join donors and committees across Ohio campaign finance data. <span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="">Hank-assisted</a></span> resolution pipelines that use Jev as the workhorse reduced model costs by <strong>99.56%</strong> and increased measured call-time throughput to 7.35× the baseline while <strong>retaining near-Fable quality</strong>.</p>
<p>But it&#x27;s not all roses. Applying the wrong signal or prompting the wrong way causes large mistakes at scale. No free lunches, only subsidised ones.</p>
<p>We&#x27;ll talk about the results, <span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="#the-job" class="">explain the task of entity resolution</a></span>, and at the end we&#x27;ll provide some prompts and principles that can work for integrating models like Jev into AI data pipelines.</p>

<p>On a segment of the Ohio dataset that we selected to be difficult, using Fable to join entities costs $9.83 for 1.2 MB of prepared evidence, and takes 844.64 seconds.</p>
<p>An optimized <span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/concepts/hanks/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="">hank</a></span> (like the one below) is an alternative to direct comparisons using a model or a code-based approach. Here, it reduces model costs to $0.3012 for 715.08 seconds (a 32.6× reduction in cost but about the same time).</p>
<div class="diagram-wrapper"><figure class="jevhank" id="jev-hank" aria-label="The cheaper arm as a flow: 52 prepared batches of source evidence enter one saved Hankweave codon, decide, which runs under two model bindings — pi/openai/gpt-5.6-luna for all 52 batches and pi/google/gemini-3.7-flash for the 10 the runner refers between calls — and 199 of 200 families come out for $0.3012 and 715.08 rows</p></section><div class="jevhank-connector" aria-hidden="true"><svg class="jevhank-connector-arrow" viewBox="0 0 32 9" width="32" height="9"><path class="jevhank-connector-line" d="M0 4.5H30M26 cap · 8 unpriced</p></section><p class="jevhank-referral"><span class="jevhank-referral-edge" aria-hidden="true"><span class="jevhank-referral-dash"></span></span><span class="jevhank-referral-label">10<!-- --> of <!-- -->52<!-- --> referred</span><span class="jevhank-fact"><span aria-hidden="true">· </span>42<!-- --> of <!-- -->52<!-- --> kept</span></p><section class="jevhank-binding"><p class="jevhank-fact jevhank-model">pi/google/gemini-3.7-flash</p><p class="jevhank-fact">the 10 referred · medium thinking</p><p class="jevhank-fact jevhank-ran">10 calls · The runner binds the model, not the hank.</p></section><div class="jevhank-connector" aria-hidden="true"><svg class="jevhank-connector-arrow" viewBox="0 0 32 9" width="32" height="9"><path class="jevhank-connector-line" d="M0 4.5H30M26 1L30 4.5L26 8"></path><circle class="jevhank-connector-dot" cx="2.5" cy="4.5" r="2.5"></circle></svg></div><section class="jevhank-stage"><p class="jevhank-stage-label">families out</p><p class="jevhank-stage-figure jevhank-matched">199<!-- --> of <!-- -->200</p><p class="jevhank-fact">$0.3012</p><p class="jevhank-fact">715.08 s</p><p class="jevhank-fact">8<!-- --> unpriced</p></section></div><p class="jevhank-strip"><span class="jevhank-strip-item">budget per call · <!-- -->300<!-- --> s deadline · <!-- -->16,384<!-- --> output tokens · fail on exceed</span><span class="jevhank-strip-item">every attempt kept · prompt · response · session log · accounting</span></p></div><p class="jevhank-footer"><span class="jevhank-footer-source">hank.json · hankweave 0.10.0</span><a class="jevhank-docs" href="https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/concepts/hanks/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">What is a hank?</a></p></div><figcaption class="jevhank-caption">After Gemini Flash stopped being priced like a flash model, Luna has been a solid workhorse data-processing model for us on the Pareto frontier.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>Using only Jev to adjudicate drops accuracy significantly, but Jev as the primary workhorse inside a five-family review stage with Luna provides <strong>226x lower cost</strong> ($0.0000361 per KB), <strong>7.35x higher throughput</strong> (10.5 KBps in call-seconds against Fable&#x27;s 1.4), while being within 0.5 percentage points of Fable in accuracy.</p>
<p>Jev is the final missing piece for <span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="/blog/southbridge-scalable-data-substrates" class="">something we set out to do</a></span> 18 months ago; to scale these workflows up to Terabytes of data.</p>
<div class="diagram-wrapper"><figure id="jev-scale-gap" class="jevscale jevscale-gap" aria-label="Model costs at 1 TB"><ul class="jevscale-bars" aria-label="Extrapolated model costs at 1 TB"><li class="jevscale-bar-row" data-system="fable"><span class="jevscale-bar-name">Fable</span><span class="jevscale-bar-track" role="img" aria-label="Fable at 1 TB: $8.16m of model cost, the full width of this axis"><span class="jevscale-bar-fill" style="width:100.000%"></span></span><span class="jevscale-bar-value">$8.16m</span></li><li class="jevscale-bar-row" data-system="five-reviews"><span class="jevscale-bar-name">Jev + 5 Luna reviews</span><span class="jevscale-bar-track" role="img" aria-label="Jev + 5 Luna reviews at 1 TB: $36.1k total model cost"><span class="jevscale-bar-fill" style="width:0.442%"></span></span><span class="jevscale-bar-value">$36.1k</span><span class="jevscale-bar-parts">Jev $27.9k + Luna $8.13k</span></li></ul><figcaption class="jevscale-caption-line">Extrapolated model costs at 1 TB</figcaption></figure></div>
<div class="diagram-wrapper"><figure id="jev-grid" class="jevgrid" aria-label="Family outcomes on the 200-family measured panel. Jev only: 1 mistake and 4 declined of 200 families, 3.37¢. Positions are arbitrary; the counts and rates are measured.</desc><g data-method="jev-only" transform="translate(0, 0)" class="jevgrid-col"><text class="jevgrid-name" x="0" y="15">Jev only</text><rect class="jevgrid-dot" x="0" y="24" width="5" height="5" rx="1"></rect><rect class="jevgrid-dot jevgrid-abstain" x="8" y="24" width="5" height="5" rx="1" tabindex="0" role="button" aria-label="Jev only: Declined to certify a single-row donor. Both were typed correctly as a person. Jev answered &quot;uncertain&quot; on whether one lone contribution row is a coherent donor unit (0.57 and 0.56), so the atom carries an uncertainty flag the reference does not. 72.6931C58.4262 77.649 59.9328 81.9654 61.4395 83.5642C62.6452 84.8431 63.549 85.1629 63.8499 85.1629C67.228 83.0121 68.2585 79.2055 70.9308 76.3701C75.1489 71.8937 75.9422 71.2958 81.9278 21.375L171.213 21.3396C167.093 18.5784 159.105 13.2249 154.213 12.576C150.598 12.0964 151.078 12.2624 149.42 11.623C139.424 7.76541 134.213 0.580763 122.166 0.0248927C113.191 -0.389138 104.808 4.37634 100.458 13.2216C98.6505 16.8986 99.0543 18.2543 97.7476 20.2673C96.2315 22.6044 85.8249 24.8915 82.8688 25.5304C71.8889 27.9035 67.407 29.6406 56.9195 33.8447C50.1405 36.5626 43.813 41.1988 39.5949 44.0764Z"></path><path d="M124.717 36.6905C129.626 36.6905 133.605 32.1812 133.605 26.6187C133.605 21.0562 129.626 16.5469 124.717 16.5469C119.808 16.5469 115.828 21.0562 115.828 26.6187C115.828 32.1812 119.808 36.6905 124.717 36.6905Z"></path></svg></button>The job</h2>
<p>The task is simple. Can we resolve entities across the <span class="link-preview-wrapper relative inline"><a href="https://www.ohiosos.gov/campaign-finance/search/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" class="">Ohio Campaign Finance dataset</a></span>? Entities here could be donors, committees, companies, etc. This is the task we have been working on as part of a much larger ingestion and data pipelining test designed to measure 4a, our internal superagent that can autonomously build and self-optimize AI data pipelines.</p>
<p>In practice, ER is incredibly difficult. Humans make honest mistakes - middle names are a common example.</p>

























<div class="table-wrapper"><table node="[object Object]"><thead><tr><th>Filing A</th><th>Filing B</th><th>Same person?</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>DANIEL R. OKAFOR</td><td>DANIEL OKAFOR JR</td><td>A middle initial on one record, a suffix on the other; same street address.</td></tr><tr><td>KAREN L.</td><td>KAREN L</td><td>An initial and punctuation inside the given-name field.</td></tr><tr><td>WALTER H. BRENNAN SR.</td><td>WANDA BRENNAN</td><td>Shared surname and address, but two different given names.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p>We also move houses and jobs, change names, get married, omit information, and overall shenaniganize our lives.</p>
<p>Then there&#x27;s (alleged) hostile obfuscation - large donors and companies attempting to spread out detection with different entity names, honest <em>looking</em> mistakes, etc etc.</p>
<p>Our ER pipeline resolves these problems using <strong>atoms</strong> - bundles of equivalent donor evidence. We put rows together into atoms, and models decide on what these bundles are (a company, a person, a committee, a joint donor or an unnamed record), and how they&#x27;re related (same person, same household?). As we join more and more atoms, the dataset slowly resolves itself.</p>
<p>Here&#x27;s one case: <strong>11 rows, five atoms, two people</strong>. Ordinary code makes the atoms and keeps every original row. Jev judges which atoms represent the same donor, then whether the two donors share a household. The household is a connection between people, not permission to merge them.</p>
<div class="diagram-wrapper diagram-bleed"><figure class="jev-resolution" id="jev-resolution" aria-label="How 11 source rows become 5 atoms and 2 people, and how a person ID is joined back onto every original row."><div class="jev-resolution-scroll" tabindex="0" role="region" aria-label="Resolution diagram; scroll horizontally on small screens"><svg id="jev-resolution-graph" viewBox="0 0 960 438" role="img" aria-label="11 original rows form 5 atoms. <p>This is where Jev comes in.</p>
<p>If you were so inclined (either rich or a frontier lab), you could have a frontier LLM adjudicate <em>every</em> atom and bundle. However - even if you could pay for all of this (our estimate for the four-file Ohio snapshot is <strong>about $9,614</strong> for Fable) - speed makes it difficult to do so. Even the best of us only have about 3 billion seconds of life.</p>
<p>Additionally, we have found that at scale, using cheaper models with additional review steps can <em>surpass</em> the accuracy of even frontier models deployed raw.</p>

<p>Here are the things we learned making Jev useful for this task.</p>
<ol>
<li node="[object Object]">Telling Jev what counts as enough evidence. Our first questions spent too much time telling it what <em>wasn&#x27;t</em> proof.</li>
</ol>
<p>This was the original <code>yes</code> criterion for a household link:</p>
<div class="code-block-wrapper"><div class="code-block-container"><div class="code-block-holes" aria-hidden="true"><div class="paper-hole" style="top:52px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:73px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:94px"></div></div><div class="code-block-header"><div class="code-block-actions"><button class="code-block-wrap active" aria-label="Disable word wrap" aria-pressed="true" title="Disable word wrap"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" is supported between distinct compatible entities.</code></div></div></div></div>
<p>This is the criterion we replaced it with:</p>
<div class="code-block-wrapper"><div class="code-block-container"><div class="code-block-holes" aria-hidden="true"><div class="paper-hole" style="top:52px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:73px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:94px"></div></div><div class="code-block-header"><div class="code-block-actions"><button class="code-block-wrap active" aria-label="Disable word wrap" aria-pressed="true" title="Disable word wrap"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" style="opacity:1"><line x1="3" y1="6" x2="21" y2="6"></line><path d="M3 12h15a3 3 0 1 1 0 6h-4"></path><polyline points="13 16 16 19 13 22" transform="rotate(180 14.5 19)"></polyline><line x1="3" y1="18" x2="10" y2="18"></line></svg><span class="code-block-wrap-text">Wrap</span></button><button class="code-block-copy" aria-label="Copy code" title="Copy to clipboard"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="9" y="9" width="13" height="13" rx="2" ry="2"></rect><path d="M5 15H4a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h9a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v1"></path></svg><span class="code-block-copy-text">Copy</span></button></div><span class="code-block-language">Text</span></div><div class="code-block-content wrapped"><div style="color:#3c3836;background:transparent;font-family:&#x27;Departure Mono&#x27;, &#x27;SF Mono&#x27;, &#x27;Monaco&#x27;, monospace;font-size:14px;text-align:left;white-space:pre-wrap;word-spacing:normal;word-break:normal;word-wrap:normal;line-height:1.5;tab-size:2;padding:0;margin:0;overflow:visible"><code style="color:#3c3836;background:transparent;font-family:&#x27;Departure Mono&#x27;, &#x27;SF Mono&#x27;, &#x27;Monaco&#x27;, monospace;font-size:14px;text-align:left;white-space:pre-wrap;word-spacing:normal;word-break:normal;word-wrap:normal;line-height:1.5;tab-size:2;letter-spacing:0;padding:0">Both records give the same residential street address (same house number and street), and the two are distinct persons.</code></div></div></div></div>
<p>The revised instructions also say that <code>DR</code> and <code>DRIVE</code> don&#x27;t break an address match, and that a shared employer, business address or PO box doesn&#x27;t establish a household. On the same 13 development questions, Jev went from answering <strong>no to all 13</strong> to <strong>yes to all 13</strong>, matching all 13 reference answers. Those are development results, not the final benchmark score.</p>
<ol start="2">
<li node="[object Object]">We made the same change to identity. Here is the actual revised <code>same</code> criterion:</li>
</ol>
<div class="code-block-wrapper"><div class="code-block-container"><div class="code-block-holes" aria-hidden="true"><div class="paper-hole" style="top:52px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:73px"></div><div class="paper-hole" style="top:94px"></div></div><div class="code-block-header"><div class="code-block-actions"><button class="code-block-wrap active" aria-label="Disable word wrap" aria-pressed="true" title="Disable word wrap"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" 19)"></polyline><line x1="3" y1="18" x2="10" y2="18"></line></svg><span class="code-block-wrap-text">Wrap</span></button><button class="code-block-copy" aria-label="Copy code" title="Copy to clipboard"><svg width="14" height="14" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><rect x="9" y="9" width="13" height="13" rx="2" ry="2"></rect><path d="M5 15H4a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h9a2 2 0 0 1 2 2v1"></path></svg><span class="code-block-copy-text">Copy</span></button></div><span class="code-block-language">Text</span></div><div class="code-block-content wrapped"><div style="color:#3c3836;background:transparent;font-family:&#x27;Departure Mono&#x27;, &#x27;SF Mono&#x27;, &#x27;Monaco&#x27;, monospace;font-size:14px;text-align:left;white-space:pre-wrap;word-spacing:normal;word-break:normal;word-wrap:normal;line-height:1.5;tab-size:2;padding:0;margin:0;overflow:visible"><code style="color:#3c3836;background:transparent;font-family:&#x27;Departure Mono&#x27;, &#x27;SF Mono&#x27;, &#x27;Monaco&#x27;, monospace;font-size:14px;text-align:left;white-space:pre-wrap;word-spacing:normal;word-break:normal;word-wrap:normal;line-height:1.5;tab-size:2;letter-spacing:0;padding:0">The same donor. Sufficient: the same surname and the same or clerically equivalent given name (spelling, nickname, initial, or a middle name or suffix present on only one record) at the same residential street address, or at the same postal code with the same employer. Differences only in employer/occupation, one blank field, or address formatting do not distinguish donors.</code></div></div></div></div>
<p>Much like prompting in the 3.5-turbo days, more examples and more specific choices make things easier. Same for humans: we all prefer MCQs over essays!</p>

<p>More work remains to be done in integrating intelligence classifiers across data problems, especially when it comes to pipelining the raw performance on offer. This is the largest change we&#x27;ve seen in architecture since the flash (gemini, deepseek, glm) series of models to change how we structure data work in production. We are already seeing significant bumps in accuracy, cost and speed across other tasks like mining, selection, sanitization, and a lot more. We&#x27;ll share results as we can make them ready for publication.</p>

items-center justify-between\"}]}]\n26:T1d85,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"\nJev ([TypeSafe's system-one model](https://docs.typesafe.ai/models)) is a quantum leap forward for data processing pipelines, if harnessed correctly. We used Jev to accelerate an entity resolution pipeline to join donors and committees across Ohio campaign finance data. [Hank-assisted](https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/) resolution pipelines that use Jev as the workhorse reduced model costs by **99.56%** and increased measured call-time throughput to 7.35× the baseline while **retaining near-Fable quality**.\n\nBut it's not all roses. Applying the wrong signal or prompting the wrong way causes large mistakes at scale. No free lunches, only subsidised ones.\n\nWe'll talk about the results, [explain the task of entity resolution](#the-job), and at the end we'll provide some prompts and principles that can work for integrating models like Jev into AI data pipelines.\n\n## Results\n\n```diagram\njev-flat-bubble bleed\n```\n\nOn a segment of the Ohio dataset that we selected to be difficult, using Fable to join entities costs \\$9.83 for 1.2 MB of prepared evidence, and takes 844.64 seconds.\n\nAn optimized [hank](https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/concepts/hanks/) (like the one below) is an alternative to direct comparisons using a model or a code-based approach. Here, it reduces model costs to \\$0.3012 for 715.08 seconds (a 32.6× reduction in cost but about the same time).\n\n```diagram\njev-hank\n```\n\nUsing only Jev to adjudicate drops accuracy significantly, but Jev as the primary workhorse inside a five-family review stage with Luna provides **226x lower cost** (\\$0.0000361 per KB), **7.35x higher throughput** (10.5 KBps in call-seconds against Fable's 1.4), while being within 0.5 percentage points of Fable in accuracy.\n\nJev is the final missing piece for [something we set out to do](/blog/southbridge-scalable-data-substrates) 18 months ago; to scale these workflows up to Terabytes of data.\n\n```diagram\njev-scale-gap\n```\n\n```diagram\njev-grid\n```\n\n## The job\n\nThe task is simple. Can we resolve entities across the [Ohio Campaign Finance dataset](https://www.ohiosos.gov/campaign-finance/search/)? Entities here could be donors, committees, companies, etc. This is the task we have been working on as part of a much larger ingestion and data pipelining test designed to measure 4a, our internal superagent that can autonomously build and self-optimize AI data pipelines.\n\nIn practice, ER is incredibly difficult. Humans make honest mistakes - middle names are a common example.\n\n| Filing A | Filing B | Same person? |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| DANIEL R. OKAFOR | DANIEL OKAFOR JR | A middle initial on one record, a suffix on the other; same street address. |\n| KAREN L. | KAREN L | An initial and punctuation inside the given-name field. |\n| WALTER H. BRENNAN SR. | WANDA BRENNAN | Shared surname and address, but two different given names. |\n\nWe also move houses and jobs, change names, get married, omit information, and overall shenaniganize our lives.\n\nThen there's (alleged) hostile obfuscation - large donors and companies attempting to spread out detection with different entity names, honest *looking* mistakes, etc etc.\n\nOur ER pipeline resolves these problems using **atoms** - bundles of equivalent donor evidence. We put rows together into atoms, and models decide on what these bundles are (a company, a person, a committee, a joint donor or an unnamed record), and how they're related (same person, same household?). As we join more and more atoms, the dataset slowly resolves itself.\n\nHere's one case: **11 rows, five atoms, two people**. Ordinary code makes the atoms and keeps every original row. Jev judges which atoms represent the same donor, then whether the two donors share a household. The household is a connection between people, not permission to merge them.\n\n```diagram\njev-resolution bleed\n```\n\nThis is where Jev comes in.\n\nIf you were so inclined (either rich or a frontier lab), you could have a frontier LLM adjudicate *every* atom and bundle. However - even if you could pay for all of this (our estimate for the four-file Ohio snapshot is **about \\$9,614** for Fable) - speed makes it difficult to do so. Even the best of us only have about 3 billion seconds of life.\n\nAdditionally, we have found that at scale, using cheaper models with additional review steps can *surpass* the accuracy of even frontier models deployed raw.\n\n## Prompts\n\nHere are the things we learned making Jev useful for this task.\n\n1. Telling Jev what counts as enough evidence. Our first questions spent too much time telling it what *wasn't* proof.\n\nThis was the original `yes` criterion for a household link:\n\n```text wrap\nThis specific relationship is supported between distinct compatible entities.\n```\n\nThis is the criterion we replaced it with:\n\n```text wrap\nBoth records give the same residential street address (same house number and street), and the two are distinct persons.\n```\n\nThe revised instructions also say that `DR` and `DRIVE` don't break an address match, and that a shared employer, business address or PO box doesn't establish a household. On the same 13 development questions, Jev went from answering **no to all 13** to **yes to all 13**, matching all 13 reference answers. Those are development results, not the final benchmark score.\n\n2. We made the same change to identity. Here is the actual revised `same` criterion:\n\n```text wrap\nThe same donor. Sufficient: the same surname and the same or clerically equivalent given name (spelling, nickname, initial, or a middle name or suffix present on only one record) at the same residential street address, or at the same postal code with the same employer. Differences only in employer/occupation, one blank field, or address formatting do not distinguish donors.\n```\n\nMuch like prompting in the 3.5-turbo days, more examples and more specific choices make things easier. Same for humans: we all prefer MCQs over essays!\n\n## Conclusion\n\nMore work remains to be done in integrating intelligence classifiers across data problems, especially when it comes to pipelining the raw performance on offer. This is the largest change we've seen in architecture since the flash (gemini, deepseek, glm) series of models to change how we structure data work in production. We are already seeing significant bumps in accuracy, cost and speed across other tasks like mining, selection, sanitization, and a lot more. We'll share results as we can make them ready for publication.\n\n## Data\n\nYou can download the publication-safe experiment data and the Ohio campaign-finance sources here.\n\n- [Costs, clocks and workload data](/files/jev-entity-resolution/economics.json)\n- [Research results, including repeat runs and other trials](/files/jev-entity-resolution/research-results.json)\n- [The illustrated case, with invented identifying values](/files/jev-entity-resolution/resolution-example.json)\n- [Exact prompt excerpts](/files/jev-entity-resolution/prompts.json)\n- [Runnable seven-row example and full offline report](/files/jev-entity-resolution/study.zip) — extract the bundle, then run `bun example.ts --dry-run` from the `publication` folder. This makes no model call. The small example demonstrates classification and joining labels back to rows, not the full resolver.\n- [Ohio's public campaign-finance search and downloads](https://www.ohiosos.gov/campaign-finance/search/)\n\nWant to try this on your own data? Start with [Jev's typed questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice), and use [Hankweave](https://hankweave.southbridge.ai/) for the reasoning steps.\n\n"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"20:[\"$\",\"main\",null,{\"className\":\"flex-1 py-12 md:py-16
